title: Dogs evolved puppy-dog eyes
hook: Dogs have an eyebrow muscle that wolves mostly lack, and it works on us.
peek: A 2019 study found that dogs have a small muscle that lifts the inner eyebrow, making the sad, wide-eyed look we call puppy-dog eyes. Wolves mostly lack it, which suggests the muscle spread because people respond to it.
lede: When a dog raises its inner eyebrows, its eyes look bigger and a little sad, a bit like a human baby or a worried face. In 2019 a team led by psychologist Juliane Kaminski compared the faces of dogs and wolves. They found that dogs reliably have a muscle that makes this expression, while wolves mostly do not.

bullets.text: The muscle is called the levator anguli oculi medialis. In the dogs the team dissected it was well developed, while in wolves it was usually only a few scattered fibres, too weak to make the same movement.
The researchers also filmed dogs and wolves meeting a person. Dogs raised their inner eyebrows more often and more intensely, while wolves rarely made the movement at all.

An earlier study by the same group found that shelter dogs that raised their inner eyebrows more often were rehomed sooner. That gives a plausible route for the trait to spread: people favoured dogs that made it.
Dogs split from wolves within roughly the last 30,000 years, a short time for a new facial muscle to appear. The authors suggest people's unconscious preference for the look may have sped it along.
